One person

Eighteen months. Four programs. Four agencies.

January

Emergency shelter

Agency A

Reported: 42 bed nights

Spring

Mental health program

Agency B

Reported: completed

Summer

Employment service

Agency C

Next winter

Housing

Agency D

Four intake forms. Four sets of outcome numbers. Four funders. Every report is accurate.

Not one of them can say whether this person's life stabilized, or what it took to get there.

Programs report moments. People live movement.

Shelter 88%, mental health 81%, employment 84%, housing 90%. Every funder report reads as a success.

Neither view is wrong. They answer different questions. Only the second one tells you who is stuck, where, and for how long.
Illustrative figures, not any organization's data. Published returns: 16.6 to 19.7 percent of exits to permanent housing within 24 months (HUD, FY2020 to 2024); 22.1 to 24.3 percent of all shelter leavers within a year, BC, Ontario and Nova Scotia shelters in HICC data (2025). Housing First with assertive community treatment: high-needs participants stably housed 71 percent of the time, 29 percent for usual care, over 24 months (Aubry et al., 2016).
HelpSeeker  Crisis to stabilityMareto04
You asked: outcomes or impact?

Outputs, outcomes, impact

Output

What we did

120 bed nights. 14 counselling sessions. One job placement.

Measured by counting activity.

Outcome

What changed while we were involved

Moved from shelter into a lease. Fewer crisis calls this quarter.

Measured by comparing entry and exit, inside one program.

Impact

What changed and lasted

Still housed and connected a year after every program closed.

Measured by following the person after discharge, across agencies.

The practical line: you cannot see impact from inside one program. In the data, impact is an outcome whose measurement date sits after the case closed. Journey measurement is how outcome data becomes impact evidence.
Definitions follow OECD (2023), Glossary of key terms in evaluation and results based management, 2nd ed., pp. 36 and 45; Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat, Policy on Results, Appendix A; W.K. Kellogg Foundation (2004), Logic model development guide, p. 2.
HelpSeeker  Crisis to stabilityMareto05
Part one

Describing the journey

Three phases, the moves between them, and the places people disappear.
01
Tool one

Three phases, and what you can actually record

PhaseWhat it looks likeSignals you can recordWhere the data comes from
CrisisImmediate safety and basic needsShelter stay, crisis call, emergency visit, detox admissionShelter, crisis line, outreach, hospital partners
StabilizationBuilding the supports that make the next step possibleEnrolled in ongoing support, income in place, housing search active, goals setCase management, mental health, income and employment programs
RecoveryHolding the gains after formal supports step backHoused at follow-up, no crisis contact in the period, own goal ratings holdingFollow-up contact, housing provider, the person themselves
Phase is a judgement made from recorded signals, not a box a worker ticks from memory. Agree the signals once and the phase follows from the data.

The insight most frameworks miss

Count the moves, not just the states

Crisissafety and basic needs
arrow_forward
Stabilizationsupports in place
arrow_forward
Recoverygains holding
u_turn_leftReturns to crisis are part of the journey. Count them, do not hide them.

Moving forward

How many people moved from crisis to stabilization, and how long it took.

Holding

How many reached recovery and were still there at the next follow-up.

Exits to unknown

Record where people go, including "unknown". If unknown is your biggest category, that is your first finding.

Across shelters in BC, Ontario and Nova Scotia that share data with HICC, 53.7 to 63.3 percent of exits each year from 2018-19 to 2023-24 had an unknown reason (HICC, 2025). Returns are expected in recovery: Prochaska, DiClemente and Norcross (1992); Mental Health Commission of Canada (2014), At Home/Chez Soi National Final Report, p. 27.

1  The handoff

Weeks between one discharge and the next intake. No program owns them, so no program measures them.

2  The quiet return

A step back toward crisis at another agency reads as a brand new client. The system learns nothing.

3  After discharge

Recovery is where the outcome is decided, and where reporting usually stops.

Illustrative journey. Transitions carry risk: death 12.7 times more likely than in the general population in the first two weeks after release from prison, Washington State (Binswanger et al., 2007); suicide 1,132 per 100,000 person-years in the three months after psychiatric discharge against 484 overall (Chung et al., 2017).
HelpSeeker  Crisis to stabilityMareto09
Part two

Measuring movement

Five measures, each defined tightly enough to calculate.
02
Tool two

Five measures of movement

MeasureHow to calculate itWhat it tells you
Time to stabilizationDays from first crisis contact to first enrolment in ongoing supportHow fast the system connects people once they surface
Handoff gapDays between exit from one program and entry to the nextWhere people wait, and which handoffs fail
Return to crisisShare of people who reached stabilization and had a crisis contact within 6 or 12 monthsWhether gains hold, and for whom
Recovery holdShare of people in recovery at discharge who are still there at the 6 and 12 month follow-upThe closest practical proxy for impact
Self-rated progressChange in the person's own goal ratings, by domain, from intake to each reviewWhether life is improving by their definition, not only ours
Each one needs a date and a person ID that matches across services. That is why the data foundation in part three matters more than any dashboard.
Time to stabilization follows HUD System Performance Measure 1; return windows of 6, 12 and 24 months follow Measure 2; Reaching Home lists returns as a required outcome. "Handoff gap" is a measure we propose; no published source defines it. Self-rating: Goal Attainment Scaling (Steenbeek et al., 2010) and Goal-Based Outcomes (Edbrooke-Childs et al., 2015), evidence from paediatric and child mental health settings.

HelpSeeker  Crisis to stabilityMareto12
Part three

The data foundation

The same person across services, shared definitions, and consent that keeps up.
03
Tool three

The minimum journey dataset

Ten fields. You probably collect several already, just not consistently or in a form that can be joined across services.

FieldWhy it matters
1. Person IDThe one thing every other measure depends on
2. Program and agencyWhich part of the system each step happened in
3. Start and end datesTurns enrolments into a timeline and gaps
4. Referred from and toShows the handoff, not just two separate files
5. Exit destinationIncluding "unknown", counted honestly
FieldWhy it matters
6. Housing statusUsing a shared definition across partners
7. Phase at entry and exitDerived from agreed signals
8. Consent scope and dateWhat can be shared, with whom, until when
9. Goals and self-ratingsThe person's definition of progress
10. Follow-up date and resultThe only way to see recovery
Five of the ten fields (person ID, program, dates, referral, exit destination) appear in both HUD's HMIS data standards (FY 2026) and HIFIS; housing status and consent are recorded in HIFIS; phase, goals with self-ratings, consent as a history and the follow-up result are additions.

Wireframe: the duplicate check at a partner's intake. Fictional person and agencies.
Statistics Canada linked 95.87 percent of cancer registry records to its population depository, with 97.74 percent sensitivity and 99.36 percent specificity, using names, date of birth, date of death, sex, postal code and municipality (2018); shelter records carry fewer identifiers, so expect lower rates. Two or three indirect identifiers plus the service provider's identifier reach 95 percent sensitivity and 98 percent specificity (Setoguchi et al., 2014).
HelpSeeker  Crisis to stabilityMareto15
Shared definitions

Do not invent definitions. Adopt one that exists.

The problem

"Housed" means three things

Agency A counts a shelter bed. Agency B counts a lease. Agency C counts couch surfing with family. Add the totals together and the number means nothing.

The fix: a written list of categories every partner uses, ideally one your funders already recognize.

Example: the Canadian Definition of Homelessness
UnshelteredLiving on the street or in places not meant for people
Emergency shelteredStaying in emergency shelters
Provisionally accommodatedTemporary, without security of tenure
At risk of homelessnessHoused, but precariously

Movement between categories becomes a measure everyone can read the same way.

Gaetz, S. et al. (2012, revised 2017). Canadian Definition of Homelessness. Canadian Observatory on Homelessness.

Tool four

A consent model that keeps up with the journey

1

Within our agency

The default. Staff who serve the person see what they need.

2

Named partners, named purpose

"Housing details to the employment service." Scoped by agency and by type of information.

3

Counted, never named

Included in aggregate journey reports, with small numbers suppressed.

4

Reviewed and withdrawable

Revisited at set points. Withdrawal from one partner takes effect everywhere at once.

History

Jan 12 granted  |  Jul 10 renewed  |  Jul 15 scoped  |  Sep 2 withdrawn for one partner
Wireframe: consent recorded as a history, not a single checkbox. Fictional person and agencies.
HIFIS already records consent as typed records rather than a checkbox, a Canadian precedent (HICC, 2025); the four levels here are HelpSeeker's design. Revisiting consent over time follows the dynamic consent literature (Kaye et al., 2015; Teare et al., 2021). CAN/DGSI 100-11:2025 is the national standard for community and human services data.
HelpSeeker  Crisis to stabilityMareto17
Data sovereignty

First Nations, Inuit and Métis data governance, and OCAP®

Following a person over time means holding more of their story, for longer. When that data is from or about First Nations people, OCAP® is a design requirement from the first conversation, not a compliance step at the end.

Ownership

The community owns its information

Control

Over how it is collected, used and shared

Access

To data about themselves and their community

Possession

Physical stewardship of the data

Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami's National Inuit Strategy on Research and Métis governments set their own data principles. HelpSeeker does not restate them; the community decides what a journey measure includes.

OCAP® is a registered trademark of the First Nations Information Governance Centre (FNIGC), which describes OCAP® as First Nations principles. Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami, National Inuit Strategy on Research (2018); Métis National Council, Métis Nation Data Strategy (2025).

Four domains for the room. HelpSeeker's wellbeing ontology carries four underneath them (body, mind, heart, spirit). Purpose and meaning is the one this list leaves out; the person's own words often supply it.
HelpSeeker  Crisis to stabilityMareto20
You asked: how, without adding burden?

Measuring the journey without burdening anyone

forward

Capture once, carry forward

Details collected at the first door travel with the person, with consent. Nobody retells their story four times.

event_available

Use moments that already happen

Intake, case review, discharge, and one follow-up. No separate survey schedule.

checklist

A few questions, asked the same way

Three or four person-rated questions beat a long instrument that only gets half filled in.

visibility

Give the data back

When staff and clients can see the progress, recording it stops feeling like reporting.

Shorter questionnaires raise response, odds 1.64 postal and 1.73 electronic (Edwards et al., 2009, Cochrane, 513 trials). Progress feedback reduces dropout, OR 1.19, 58 studies (de Jong et al., 2021). Warm handoffs are contested: the largest study, 2,690 referrals, found no effect (Pace et al., 2018); three smaller ones found two to three times the attendance (Anand and Desai, 2023; Tobin et al., 2026; Readdean et al., 2026); none in homelessness services.

HelpSeeker  Crisis to stabilityMareto24
Both lenses from the same records

Program managers keep their view. The journey sits on top.

Mareto program manager view: open cases, events and members for one program. Demo instance with fictional data.
Program view: caseloads, contacts and contract reporting, exactly as funders ask for them today.
Journey view: the same people, read across programs and over time, with the five measures of movement.

No second system and no double entry. The journey is a different way of reading records you already keep: one person, cases with dates, events with types, outcomes with follow-up dates.

HelpSeeker  Crisis to stabilityMareto25
Tool five

Where are you today?

1
Counting activity

Contacts, bed nights and sessions. Reports describe what the program did.

2
Program outcomes

Change measured between entry and exit, inside each program on its own.

3
The person across your own programs

One record per person inside your organization. Internal handoffs and returns are visible.

4
The person across partners

Shared definitions and consent-based sharing with other agencies. Handoff gaps and follow-up are measured.

5
System learning

Agencies and funders plan from which sequences of support lead to stability that lasts.

In our experience, many organizations start at level 1 or 2, and moving up one level is a realistic goal for a year. This ladder is a self-check, not a validated scale.

HelpSeeker  Crisis to stabilityMareto26
If you deliver services

Where to start on Monday

1

Map one real journey

Pick one person, with consent, and draw their path across every service you know they touched. The gaps appear immediately.

2

Agree one definition

Choose one word, like housed, and write it down with one partner organization.

3

Read your consent form

Does it allow sharing that changes over time? Can someone withdraw from one partner only?

4

Add one follow-up

One structured check-in at three or six months after discharge, recorded the same way every time.

Continuing care after discharge improves outcomes, effect .19 at end and .27 at follow-up across 19 trials (Blodgett et al., 2014); quarterly recovery check-ups added 94 abstinent days over four years (Dennis and Scott, 2012); SAMHSA requires a six-month follow-up with 80 percent completion.
HelpSeeker  Crisis to stabilityMareto27
If you fund or plan a system

Four moves for funders and planners

moving

Ask for movement, not just volume

Add one journey question to your reporting template: where did people go next, and did it hold?

menu_book

Set the definitions once

Publish the shared definitions every funded agency uses, so the numbers can be added up.

event_repeat

Fund the follow-up

Recovery is only measured if someone is paid to check in after discharge.

groups

Report in aggregate, protect people

Journey reports roll up to groups, with small numbers suppressed. Identifiable records stay where consent allows.

HelpSeeker  Crisis to stabilityMareto28
Summary

Three things to take away

1

Measure people, not just programs

Program numbers capture moments. Movement shows when you follow the person, and count the moves between phases.

2

Build the foundation first

One person ID, shared definitions and a consent model that lasts. Every measure of movement depends on them.

3

Let the person define stability

Their words and their ratings, with a shared domain underneath so it still counts.
